preamble: The complete elision of the velar stop [k] is the final stage of a lenition chain that typically moves from stop to fricative to glide before disappearing entirely.

examples.note: Finnish consonant gradation: strong grade /k/ → weak grade ∅. E.g., 'puku' (suit) → 'puvun' (GEN) — though that's k→v. A cleaner k→∅: 'suku' → 'suvun' shows k→v; pure k→∅ occurs e.g. 'jokea' → 'jo-' in compounds.
Indonesian nasal prefix meN-: initial /k/ is deleted and replaced by the nasal /ŋ/ of the prefix (KPST rule: k, p, s, t deleted after nasal prefix).
Complete elision of the intervocalic velar stop.
Loss of the final velar consonant over time.

In Western Nuer dialects, word-final /k/ undergoes lenition to approximant [ɰ] or complete elision [∅], distinguishing Western Nuer from the Jikany-based standard variety which retains /k/. This represents a synchronic or recent historical sound change marking dialect divergence within the Nuer speech community.

languageExamples.language: West Sogeram languages (Madang Province, Papua New Guinea)

examples.note: A striking innovation of the West Sogeram branch (Trans-New Guinea, Madang Province) is the complete loss of all word-initial consonants from polysyllabic words, regardless of place or manner of articulation. Proto-Sogeram *k- is deleted word-initially in polysyllabic contexts. This is documented by Don Daniels (2015, A Reconstruction of Proto-Sogeram) and represents an extreme consonant-initial weakening chain beginning with k-lenition.
Single intervocalic stops are elided in Maharashtri Prakrit
Guaraní drops word-final consonants; Old Tupi keeps them with an added -a (îararaka)
RPA spelling; the final letter marks tone, not a consonant

*k is lost before the sonorants *l and *n with compensatory lengthening of the preceding vowel, but retained before obstruents (pakto 'mushroom', sokcha 'bag'); Proto-Muskogean is a reconstructed stage. Compare Choctaw and Chickasaw lakna, Mikasuki lakni.
Compare Choctaw nakni, Hitchiti-Mikasuki nakni (Martin 2001, Table 6).
Compare Mikasuki hakli, Chickasaw and Choctaw haklochi 'to hear (causative)'.

Conditioned loss of preconsonantal *k in Creek/Seminole, with the environments set out by Booker (1988); not exceptionless (sukcv 'bag', esakpv 'upper arm'). Martin (2001) treats the change as possibly shared with Alabama-Koasati.
Compare Alabama and Koasati pakto, Choctaw pakti.
Compare Alabama and Koasati itto, where the *k assimilated instead of being lost.
